newsitem.title: USA: It's rare for Washington -- a budget deal.
newsitem.headline: It's rare for Washington -- a budget deal.

text.p: Something rare happened in Washington Friday: Republicans and Democrats alike broke out in broad smiles to declare an important victory on a battlefield normally reserved for bloody fights, the budget.

Over the years the budget has been the bane of presidents and congressional leaders alike. In 1990 President George Bush lost his "No New Taxes" pledge -- and possibly the 1992 election -- in a budget conclave at Andrews Air Force Base.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich shut the government down twice, in late 1995 and early 1996, and never has fully recovered from the pounding he got over that.

It was against that backdrop that President Clinton and his top aides, and Republicans like Gingrich and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, announced that they had reached a balanced budget accord that had proved so elusive in the past.

It was the product of late-night meetings in back rooms of the Capitol, multiple phone calls between Clinton and various congressional leaders, and helped by what appears to be a budding, businesslike relationship between Clinton and Lott.
Clinton said Lott told him that with America's economy sparking along well, there was no better time than now to get the job done.

"He said, you know, when you're doing well, it's easier to balance the budget than it is when you're not. This is not going to get any easier, we have to do it now. And I said, I agree with you, and we are going to do it," Clinton said.
Lott said that even though a deal seemed imminent, he was not sure of it until he finally spoke with Clinton by phone Friday at midday.

"I felt like when I talked to him some time before noon that it was done, but where I'm from, it's never done until you say it's done, until I said, 'Mr. President, do we have an agreement?' And he said, 'Yes we have an agreement.'"
The White House negotiating team included Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles, budget director Franklin Raines, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and National Economic Council Chairman Gene Sperling.

They spent countless hours with House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich of Ohio and Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici of New Mexico, both Republicans, and Democrats Sen. Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey and Representative John Spratt of South Carolina.
"Everyone now knows where Senator Domenici's hideaway is in the Capitol, because we have been meeting there off and on over the last four weeks," Raines said.

"We all are very familiar with the snack habits of Chairman Kasich and Chairman Domenici and Senator Lautenberg and John Spratt. We're well aware of the shortest route to John Spratt's office from that hideaway in the Capitol," he said.

Sperling, who was involved in Clinton's 1993 budget plan that Republicans opposed as a bloc and only passed because Vice President Al Gore cast a tie-breaking vote, said this deal was negotiated in good faith.
"It was no one's goal to get a deal that was not going to get the support of the other side," he said.
